tagline: America's great freshwater waterfront — millions already ride the river, and the lake towns are a straight line across the water.
summary: Chicago is one of the few US cities whose downtown is built around navigable water on two axes: the Chicago River canyon through the Loop and the Lake Michigan shorefront anchored by Navy Pier, the Midwest's most-visited attraction. River architecture cruises (Wendella — in its 90th season — Shoreline Sightseeing, City Cruises) sail dozens of departures a day, and a commuter water-taxi habit already exists between Michigan Avenue and the West Loop rail stations. Across the lake, the Indiana and Michigan harbor towns — Hammond, Michigan City, New Buffalo — and Milwaukee sit 13–70 nm away over open water, while the same trips by car mean 1.5–2.5 hours around the bottom of the lake.

use_cases.title: Harbor Country express
use_cases.body: Navy Pier / DuSable Harbor to New Buffalo (~39 nm) and Michigan City (~33 nm): beat the I-94 weekend crawl with a 75–90 minute glass-smooth flight across the lake to the beach towns and wineries — the corridor the atlas already routes today.

use_cases.title: River commuter shuttle, electrified
use_cases.body: Quiet, zero-emission, near-zero-wake shuttles on the proven Michigan Avenue ↔ Ogilvie/Union water-taxi run and out to Navy Pier — restoring and extending a pandemic-reduced commuter habit on a river where wake and noise rules favor foiling.

use_cases.title: Lakefront events & corporate charters
use_cases.body: McCormick Place, Soldier Field game days, and summer festivals: premium foiling charters between 31st Street Harbor, Monroe Harbor, Navy Pier and Northwestern's Evanston shoreline move VIPs past Lake Shore Drive traffic.

use_cases.title: Chicago ↔ Milwaukee lake run
use_cases.body: Two downtown lakefronts ~70 nm apart with no direct water link since the express-ferry era — a hybrid foiling service connects the two cities' waterfronts directly, no charging infrastructure needed at the far end.

journeys.to: New Buffalo Municipal Marina (Harbor Country, MI)
journeys.today: A ~110 km drive around the bottom of the lake through Indiana on I-94 — 1 hr 45 min on a good day, well over 2 hours on summer Fridays.
journeys.with_navier: A 39 nm straight line across Lake Michigan — about 75–90 minutes of smooth, silent flight from the Loop's doorstep to the beach-town marina.

journeys.today: A crowded 20-minute walk or a slow rideshare crawl across the Loop; the legacy water taxi runs a reduced schedule.
journeys.with_navier: A quiet electric foiling shuttle down the river canyon — frequent, all-day headways, near-zero wake under the bridges, zero emissions between the skyscrapers.

journeys.today: 1.5+ hours by car or Amtrak Hiawatha via the inland corridor; no passenger service has crossed this stretch of lake in years.
journeys.with_navier: A ~70 nm open-lake run linking two downtown waterfronts directly — flown by the hybrid foiler with full range margin in both directions.

navier_fit.pioneer_ii: The urban network is all-electric: the river canyon and lakefront harbors (Navy Pier, DuSable, Monroe, Belmont, 31st St) sit within a 1–10 nm mesh, Hammond is ~13 nm, Waukegan ~29 nm, Michigan City ~33 nm and New Buffalo ~39 nm — all comfortably inside the 70 nm envelope, with DC fast-charging viable at city-owned harbor slips.
navier_fit.quanta_lr: Quanta-LR (700 nm hybrid) owns the inter-city lake runs: Chicago ↔ Milwaukee (~70 nm, at the very top of electric range, comfortable for the hybrid) and onward Great Lakes reach (Racine, Grand Haven, Saugatuck) without any far-shore charging dependency.

competitive_landscape: Chicago has one of the strongest incumbent on-water economies in North America: Wendella (90 seasons), Shoreline Sightseeing and City Cruises run packed architecture and lakefront cruises from dawn to dusk all summer, and Wendella's Chicago Water Taxi carries commuters on the river. That density is the demand evidence. What is missing is speed and point-to-point utility: every incumbent vessel is a slow displacement boat, the water-taxi network shrank after the pandemic, and nothing crosses the lake — the express-ferry era's direct city-to-city links are gone.

precedents.what: ~$100M, ~100-vessel electric foiling network with JIH Global, 3-year phased rollout, first 5 vessels in 2026
precedents.why_it_matters: Demonstrates the financed, phased fleet model — the same playbook scales down to a city network anchored on Navy Pier and the municipal harbors.

seasonality: A sharply seasonal market: the boating season runs roughly May–October (Chicago Park District harbors open mid-April to October), with winter ice and lake gales closing the off-season — fleet utilization planning should assume a concentrated 6–7 month peak, mirroring the incumbents. Within the season, Lake Michigan's notorious short-period chop is the daily pain for conventional boats; foiling above it converts marginal-weather days into smooth, runnable schedule — extending the effective season at both ends.
regulatory_note: US-flag passenger service under US Coast Guard small-passenger-vessel rules (Subchapter T/K) and Jones Act US-build requirements for domestic routes. The operating environment actively favors clean vessels: EPA and bi-national Great Lakes water-quality programs, Chicago's river-revitalization agenda, and wake/noise sensitivity in the river canyon make a zero-emission, near-zero-wake foiling fleet a regulatory fit rather than a hurdle. The Chicago Park District (harbors) and the city's riverwalk authority control most boarding infrastructure.
